items.title: Stanley Dance interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 12, 1998
items.q: And I said something about this growl. And Ian says, “You growl on a trumpet, Stanley, or a trombone, not on a saxophone.”

ctx.x: Well radio of course. You’d hear jazz of the time on the radio. Then by a lucky chance, my father sent me away to a boarding school, where the sons of several of the directors of the leading record companies were also sent. Now these kids came back each term with all the records. Most kids brought back the records they liked, which was the pop records, and you’d be sick of them you know after two or three times. But these kids would have weird records by Jelly Roll Morton and his Hot Peppers. We were very fond of…

from this grew a sort of more intelligent interest in music. There was, early on in England there was the paper called The Melody Maker which had record reviews which were fairly hip. But the influence in England to begin with was mainly coming from, well very often came from New York musicians who were playing in The Savoy Hotel and places like that. They came over and they were full of we’ll say Red Nichols, Joe Venuti, Ed Lang and people like that. But the black musicians were considered, for a long time,…

then I think the next, oh it would be ‘37, a friend and I gathered up the money to go to New York the cheapest way possible on the Queen Mary, you know, right in the front of this big old ship which was about 40 pounds round trip or something you know.
